39: This plan describes a counter-service rotisserie chicken restaurant, Peruvian style (pollo a la brasa): two commercial gas rotisseries with 8 spits each (the rods the chickens are loaded on) in plain view from the street, a counter with a heated display and pre-orders, and {{aforo}} seats with no table service. One clarification: in the United States a poultry store sells raw chicken, and this plan is about cooked chicken served to the guest. It opens in a residential neighborhood of a mid-sized American city of 150,000 to 300,000 people, in a second-generation restaurant space of about 1,600 sq ft (149 sq m) with a Type I hood and an exhaust duct to the roof, easy parking and a quick pickup. It is run by a single-owner LLC, with you as general manager and head of the rotisserie. It opens seven days a week, starting in January, and Sunday is the peak.
40: The key figures of the example case are these. We average {{clientes_dia}} covers a day across the counter, the dining room, take-out, pre-orders and delivery, at an average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, over {{dias}} opening days. A family meal counts as 3.5 covers. That produces {{ventas_a1}} in year-1 revenue and a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, or {{margen_neto_a1}} of sales. The average includes the ramp-up: the Excel spreads the year month by month, and Month 1 is January, one of the softest months, so the start falls on the low part of the year. Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, and cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments, is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}}. That is a modest return, not a guaranteed one: it is a starting point for you to change the assumptions and put in your own numbers.
41: Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} for build-out, hood, rotisseries, equipment and opening, which includes the security deposit and {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before opening, plus a {{fondo_maniobra}} working capital reserve. The cash needed at opening comes to {{necesidad_caja}}. It is funded with {{fondos_propios}} of your own money ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with no interest-only period. The annual loan payment is {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax is collected from guests and passed on to the state, so it never enters the investment.
42: From there, covers grow {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3 at the same average check, and the team grows with them, so revenue rises to {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}, and net profit to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. The margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}} in year 1, and the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) never falls below {{dscr_min}} over the life of the loan, against the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders typically look for. Payback before debt comes from the cash flow in the Excel: {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted in the investment, and {{payback_capex}} on startup costs alone.
43: The team is small and leans on you. You are the general manager and head of the rotisserie, and you run the spits every day. With you are a second rotisserie cook, a prep and relief rotisserie cook who covers days off, a counter lead who also works the register, part-time counter, packing and expo staff, dish and prep help and a fry and line cook for weekends and peak days: {{plantilla_puestos}} people on the payroll who add up to {{plantilla_jornadas_xl}} full-time equivalents, all W-2 employees. The kit includes this ten-section business plan, the nine-sheet financial projections in Excel, the 80-task startup checklist in six phases, the Rotisserie Chicken Yield & Costing Calculator and the Equivalents Guide. What sets it apart is the bird and the rotisserie with real numbers: 48 birds per load on each 8-spit rotisserie and about 40 birds a day on average, climbing to 65-70 on a Sunday in the example, estimates that you measure yourself.
46: Not every chicken place is the same business, and it pays to choose before you sign anything. The weekend take-out rotisserie, open Friday through Sunday and holidays, fits in a fraction of the space, with no dining room and seasonal staff: it is the classic weekend model. The full-service Peruvian restaurant with a charcoal or wood-fired rotisserie and a big dining room needs more space, a separate exhaust and a far larger investment, and it is a different plan. A food truck serving rotisserie chicken is another model, with its own commissary and permits, and it has its own kit: the Food Truck Business Plan Kit. The one in this plan is the neighborhood counter-service rotisserie chicken restaurant with take-out, pre-orders and a small dining room, which serves the Peruvian chicken regular and the family looking for Sunday dinner.
47: The counter has to speak to five styles of rotisserie chicken, and it helps to know them because your guest brings them in their head. The Peruvian one is pollo a la brasa: a marinade of 24 to 48 hours with soy sauce, beer, garlic, cumin, aji panca, huacatay and vinegar, turned on a rotisserie, and served with yuca fries or fries, salad and sauces such as aji verde, aji amarillo and huancaina. It was born around 1950 in Lima. Then comes peri-peri, a Portuguese-style chicken with an African chile sauce. Charcoal chicken is the same bird over charcoal, the signature of the Lima rotisserie and, here, a fuel variant with its own fire rules. The French one is the poulet rôti, on horizontal spits with potatoes browning in the juices. And the Venezuelan pollo en brasa comes with garlic, cumin and annatto, yuca and guasacaca, an avocado sauce. All five are guide content with no Excel of their own: the case runs Peruvian-style chicken on gas rotisseries.
48: The case prices to the market rather than to a wish. As a kit estimate based on the menus we reviewed, the quarter chicken with two sides is $13.00, the half chicken with two sides $17.50, the family meal (a whole chicken, two large sides and two sauces) $34.00, a whole chicken on its own $19.00, an extra side $4.50, a sandwich or bowl $13.50, a soda (Peruvian golden soda or other) $3.25, a chicha morada (16 oz) $4.00 and a beer $6.50, all before sales tax. The shop sells beer and wine only, with no full liquor, and the beer and wine license is applied for early and never counted on. Everything is costed bird by bird: a marinated 3.0 lb (1.4 kg) chicken costs about $5.99 in ingredients with holding waste included, and a family meal comes to about 30% food cost (kit estimate), which is what lets it sell at a family price and still leave a margin.
49: The average check in the case is {{ticket}} per cover excluding sales tax, which is {{precio_menu}} with tax included. Because a family meal feeds about 3.5 people, the plan counts it as 3.5 covers and prices each cover from there. A typical cover is made of a share of a quarter chicken, a half or a family meal, a sandwich or bowl, an extra side or a sauce, and about 0.65 drinks, mostly sodas, Peruvian golden soda among them, and chicha morada with some beer. On an average day, roughly 55 covers eat in, 55 pick up or pre-order and 20 come through third-party delivery marketplaces (kit estimate). Food makes up {{comida_pct}} of sales and beverages {{bebida_pct}}. Marketplaces carry {{plataforma_pct}} of sales, and the rest is the counter, the dining room and direct pickup. At that check, cost of goods is {{cogs_pct_xl}} of sales, which leaves a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}.
50: A detail that saves you a headache is saying clearly what you are. This is a rotisserie chicken restaurant: a fixed-size broiler/fryer of 2.5 to 4.5 lb, well cooked and probed, Sunday pre-orders with a pickup time, combos that give you the margin and a small dining room with a Peruvian-style half chicken. It is not pressure-fried chicken (Broaster is a brand), not a fried chicken and wings place, and not a store that sells raw chicken. Do not call it pollo asado either: in the United States that means Mexican grilled chicken, the model of El Pollo Loco. Say what is on the plate and what is in each sauce, because the marinade carries soy and wheat, and aji verde and huancaina often carry egg and milk. And do not promise gluten-free if the fryer is shared with breaded items.
53: Demand for rotisserie chicken is better read through what people search for than through market-size estimates of doubtful origin, and we have none with a source here. According to DataForSEO, on October 29, 2026 Google US shows these monthly searches: pollo a la brasa 40,500, peruvian chicken 40,500, peri peri chicken 40,500, charcoal chicken 18,100, rotisserie chicken oven 4,400, peruvian rotisserie chicken 3,600, peruvian chicken restaurant 2,900, chicken rotisserie machine 2,400, rotisserie chicken restaurant 1,600 and commercial rotisserie oven 590. Read them as interest in the dish and the craft, not as sales: they say that guests look for this chicken, that the vocabulary no longer sounds strange, and that the trade searches for the equipment.
54: There is a curious gap between the person who eats and the person who opens. Guests search a lot, and most of it is people looking for dinner nearby. The person about to open searches very little: rotisserie chicken restaurant business plan, chicken restaurant business plan and how to open a chicken restaurant get about 10 searches a month each, and rotisserie chicken business about 20. It is an audience that decides with data and finds almost nothing made for its case. One word of caution on vocabulary: pollo asado gets 135,000 searches a month, but in the United States that is Mexican grilled chicken, not a synonym for rotisserie chicken, so this plan does not use it as one.
55: On prices, these are menus and guides we reviewed in October 2026, before sales tax. In a mid-sized city, a quarter chicken with two sides sits at roughly $10-13, a half chicken with two sides at $16-18 and a family meal at $31-34. That is a kit estimate: we read only two menus in full, so check the ones in your area before you set yours. One premium shop in Phoenix charges $59 for a whole bird, an outlier that does not describe the neighborhood market. Chains such as El Pollo Loco or Boston Market are not the model your guest compares you to. The anchor is the supermarket rotisserie chicken, which you cannot beat on price, so you compete on marinade, sauces and sides. The case puts the quarter at $13.00, the half at $17.50 and the family meal at $34.00, at the top of the band, which is what a new shop with the rotisseries in view needs to charge.
56: With Month 1 in January, the plan spreads sales with seasonality, and here the curve is fairly flat. January and February are the softest months, and May, July and December are the peaks: Mother's Day in May, summer cookouts and Pollo a la Brasa Day in July, and the Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve pre-orders in December. The Excel shows the spread between the best and the worst month: a neighborhood rotisserie is a fairly steady business. Month 1 in January has a consequence: the ramp-up falls on January and February, and that is why the working capital reserve counts. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row in the cash flow.
57: The gap is clear. What shows up on Google for rotisserie chicken restaurant business plan is a how-to article, forum answers, generic fast-casual templates and fried chicken franchise pages. None of them combines a fixed-location rotisserie chicken restaurant with a Word plan, an Excel that recalculates, a calculator for the cost of every bird and every plate, and a checklist. Nobody counts how many birds come off the spits before the Sunday rush, the label rules for chicken you pack for self-service, the written 4-hour hot-holding procedure for the heated display, or the leftover bird turned into the next day's sandwich. This plan does, with an Excel you can change.
58: Demand carries risks that the plan names. The price of whole chickens moves from week to week and drives your margin. A price war on whole chickens, with the chains and the supermarket rotisserie, puts pressure on the check. Marketplaces, with their commissions, eat your margin if you let them grow past the cap in the plan: the case carries {{plataforma_pct}} of sales at a commission of {{comision_pct}}. And a rotisserie that is too small falls short on Sunday. That is why it pays to have two chicken suppliers, a costing for every combo, rotisserie capacity that you measure and pickup at the counter pushed with price.
61: Before you set any price, draw the map of who competes with you in your neighborhood and your city. In rotisserie chicken the competition comes from six sides: full-service Peruvian pollo a la brasa restaurants, chain rotisserie and fast-casual chicken, the supermarket and warehouse-club rotisserie chicken, peri-peri and charcoal chicken places, fried chicken and wings shops, and the delivery marketplaces.
62: The Peruvian restaurants with a dining room compete on tradition and on a higher check, with a half chicken and sides. The chains bring brand and a purchasing scale you do not have, so you will not win a price war against them. The supermarket and warehouse-club rotisserie chicken is the price anchor in your guest's head: cheap, hot and on the way home. Peri-peri and charcoal places bring the fire and the heat. Fried chicken and wings shops fight for the same family dinner. And the marketplace is not a restaurant but a storefront where your guest compares prices in one tap and pays for delivery. Your gap is in bringing together in one place what each of them does separately: a Sunday pre-order with a pickup time, counter service, a small dining room and a Peruvian-style half chicken, made on rotisseries people can see from the street.
63: Franchise or your own brand is a calculation worth doing in writing. A franchise brings a brand, a supplier and training in exchange for the franchise fee and a monthly royalty, and its headline number is a starting point: ask for the Franchise Disclosure Document and the full investment. With your own brand, this plan puts the investment at {{inversion_total}} and you keep the margin, but you learn the craft yourself: bird size, loads, probing and Sundays. Compare the two sets of numbers with the same assumptions before you sign, and ask the franchisor about fees, royalty, advertising fund, required suppliers and exit terms.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash. Opening means plan review, a health permit and a pre-opening inspection, a building permit, a certificate of occupancy, a business license and a sales tax permit, plus a beer and wine license from the state and the city that can take months. The space is the filter: two gas rotisseries and the fryers need a Type I hood with fire suppression (UL 300) and makeup air, plus a gas service sized for them with its permit, and if the building cannot take the duct to the roof, the concept does not fit. Charcoal is solid fuel under NFPA 96 and needs its own exhaust. Ask the fire marshal in writing, because your local fire and mechanical code decides. Add the investment in build-out, rotisseries and equipment. Check everything with your city before you sign the lease.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is the product: a fixed-size bird, well cooked, probed and the same every day, and combos that leave a margin. The second is the site: a residential neighborhood near families, churches and offices, a second-generation restaurant space that can take a hood and its duct, and parking that makes pickup easy. The third is cost control: the costing of every combo and the capacity of the rotisseries, which you measure and do not assume. The fourth is the team: a steady head of the rotisserie and a counter crew that looks after the regulars who pre-order every week, because a neighbor's recommendation sells more than any ad.
66: The SWOT of this concept is clear. Strengths: a fixed-size, probed bird, Sunday pre-orders with a pickup time, combos, a Peruvian-style half chicken in the dining room and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}} in year 1. Weaknesses: a space with hood and gas requirements, a Sunday that tests the capacity of the rotisseries and a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}} that leaves little room for mistakes. Opportunities: a dish that people search for a lot, holidays and party trays for birthdays, churches and offices. Threats: the price of chicken, the price war on whole chickens and the marketplace commission. The defense for each weak point lies in two suppliers, the costing of every combo, measured capacity and pickup at the counter.
69: The marketing strategy starts in the neighborhood and follows the calendar. You open in January, and it helps to be clear about what to expect: the curious come the first month and the regular Sunday pre-orders take a quarter to build. That is why the plan does not count on a full house from day one but on a ramp. During that ramp three things carry the message: the rotisseries in view, which explain themselves from the street, a well-cooked bird at a neighborhood price and an order that is easy to place. Everything else, social media, the Google profile, combos and the stamp card, is there to turn that first visit into a second one.
70: Social media, and Instagram above all, is the showcase for the rotisserie. Post the spits loaded, the rotisseries turning, the chicken coming off and the quarter being carved in front of the camera: short videos work better than menu photos. Show how to order too, with the Sunday pickup times, the phone number and the online ordering link, because that is the part that makes a first-timer hesitate. And let people see the heated display at the hour it fills up. You do not need to post every day: a frequency you can keep is better than an opening burst that fades.
71: Your Google Business Profile is your best free ad, because nearly everyone looking for chicken nearby checks it. Complete it with photos of the rotisseries, the counter, the dining room and the chicken coming off the spit, and keep the hours current, seven days a week, with any holiday closures. Claim your Yelp page too. Reply to every review, the bad ones as well, in a calm tone and with the name of the shop. A careful reply reads like a commitment, and it counts for the guest who has not visited yet.
72: Local outreach starts at your door and in the mailbox. Pre-order cards with the phone number, flyers around the neighborhood and the number printed on every bag are the simple way to turn a neighbor into a regular Sunday guest. Party trays for birthdays, churches and offices open another door. The calendar gives you dates to work with: Mother's Day, Super Bowl Sunday, Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve for Latino families, and, in the Peruvian community, Pollo a la Brasa Day on the third Sunday of July and Fiestas Patrias on July 28. And to bring guests back, a stamp card for pre-orders. You do not need to promise conversion numbers you do not have: start with the card, measure how many get completed and adjust.
73: Marketplace or in-house delivery is a numbers decision. The plan sells {{plataforma_pct}} of its sales through third-party delivery marketplaces and pays a commission of {{comision_pct}} on those orders. Published tiers run from 15% to 30% on DoorDash and from 20% to 30% on Uber Eats, with Grubhub's marketing and delivery fees on top, plus promotions and packaging. Your own driver costs wages, employer payroll taxes, hired and non-owned auto insurance and fuel, and in most states must be a W-2 employee, so check your state. It tends to pay only with your own orders or a short, dense delivery zone, and it carries labor risk without the marketplace's storefront.
74: Pickup at the counter pays no commission, so push it with price. A small discount on an order that is picked up costs less than the marketplace commission and brings the guest to your door, where he or she sees the rotisseries and may order something more. Do the math with your own numbers. There is a product problem with delivery too: the chicken travels well in a vented container, but the fries arrive soft, so a short delivery radius helps, which is why the plan's ceiling is {{plataforma_pct}} of sales through marketplaces. There is no in-house delivery in the plan: if you ever set one up, do it with the numbers above in front of you.
75: The marketing budget in the case is {{marketing_anual}} a year, mostly for pre-order cards, flyers and the materials for the combos. The brand, website, photos and launch are separate, inside the startup costs ({{inv_lanzamiento}}). Do not spend it all at once: spread it with the calendar and keep part for the softest months, January and February, and part for the May, July and December peaks.
